activities.anchor: Data science runs on statistics whether or not it admits it
activities.caption: pair each daily artefact with its statistical engine
activities.name: statEngineMatch

config.prompt: Pair each artefact of data-science work with the statistics underneath it:

pairs.right: hypothesis testing with a dashboard attached
a sample statistic wearing confidence it has not earned

config.why: The machinery is already owned — sampling distributions, the central limit theorem, Bayes' rule — organised around the four questions a working data scientist asks.

activities.caption: call the spread of the three sessions
activities.name: statSDest

config.prompt: Session counts 4, 6 and 8 have a mean of 6. Roughly what is their standard deviation?
config.why: √(8/3) ≈ 1.63 — the root-mean-square of the deviations, which is the hinge connecting the mean to least-squares regression and the whole linear-algebra machinery of machine learning.
config.context: the deviations are −2, 0 and +2; squared, they sum to 8

activities.anchor: For bell-shaped data the empirical rule is far tighter
activities.caption: drop the marker — the two-SD share
activities.name: statEmpPlace

config.prompt: For bell-shaped data, roughly what share of values lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
config.why: About 95% within 2 SDs, 99.7% within 3 — while Chebyshev guarantees only 1 − 1/k² for any shape: at least 89% within 3 SDs, whatever the distribution.

activities.anchor: to halve the error you must
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the price of precision
activities.name: statSqrtNPredict

config.q: Your confidence interval is twice as wide as the business can act on. What must you do to the sample size?
choices: Quadruple it — the standard error shrinks with the square root of n
Double it — error scales one-to-one with sample size
Nothing — intervals shrink on their own as the metric matures
config.why: SE shrinks with √n, so halving the error takes four times the sample — the single most expensive square root in industry.

activities.anchor: Hypothesis testing is a court procedure for data
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the court's three roles
activities.name: statCourtCloze

config.text: Hypothesis testing as a court procedure: the %%0%% hypothesis is the boring defendant — nothing changed, the difference is luck; the %%1%% statistic measures how far the data sit from boring; and the %%2%%-value asks how often chance alone would produce data at least this extreme.
config.hint: The defendant, the measuring stick, and the surprise level.

activities.anchor: testing twenty metrics and reporting the winner is p-hacking
activities.caption: call the p-hacker's false-winner odds
activities.name: statHackEst

config.prompt: Testing 20 independent metrics at threshold 0.05 under a true null — what is the chance at least one looks 'significant'?
config.why: 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64% — decide the threshold and the analysis before looking, or the winner is mostly luck wearing a p-value.
config.context: one pre-declared test keeps the false-positive rate at its promised 5%

activities.anchor: the modern, more general route is the
activities.caption: the classical route versus the permutation test — drag the divider
activities.name: statPermCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to compare two groups — drag the divider:

before.label: classical
before.text: compare the difference in means against its standard error — formulas and normality assumptions

after.label: permutation
after.text: shuffle the group labels at random, recompute the difference, and score your result against what chance alone produces

config.why: No normality assumption, no formula for the statistic — the permutation test works for means, medians, conversion rates, anything computable.

activities.anchor: In a 1986 clinical study of kidney-stone treatments
activities.caption: the 78% versus 83% decision
activities.name: statKidneyBranch

config.root: Kidney-stone study, 1986: open surgery (A) succeeded on 78% of patients; the minimally invasive procedure (B) on 83%. Which treatment?

start.text: Before deciding — what do you check?

choices.label: Split by stone size
choices.feedback: Small stones: A 93% vs 87%. Large stones: A 73% vs 69%. A wins both subgroups — B's headline was inflated by its easier patient mix.

choices.label: Trust the aggregate — it has more patients
choices.feedback: The aggregate was confounded: doctors reserved open surgery for the hardest cases, so the pooled comparison compares different patient mixes.

choices.label: Randomise the next cohort of patients
choices.feedback: Random assignment breaks the link between treatment and case difficulty — the design-level fix arithmetic cannot supply.

flip.text: Treatment A wins both subgroups and loses the aggregate — Simpson's paradox in the data.

choices.label: So what repairs it?
choices.feedback: Only design: randomised assignment, so the groups are comparable before anything is aggregated.

confound.text: No amount of careful arithmetic on confounded groups repairs the confounding.

design.text: Aggregation is a modelling choice that can reverse a conclusion — the experimental-design chapter exists because of this table.

config.why: Simpson's paradox is the statistical argument for randomised design: the aggregate can be the average of several opposite stories.

activities.anchor: A companion habit: for skewed operational data
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — reading the tail
activities.name: statTailSpot

config.prompt: One of these percentile claims is backwards — click it:
lines: p50 latency describes the typical user's experience.
p95 and p99 describe the experiences a support team will hear about.
The gap between mean and p99 is a direct read of tail weight.
Dashboards that show only means reveal the tail best.
config.correction: Dashboards that show only means systematically hide the tail — and the tail is where the incidents live.
config.why: Report percentiles alongside means for skewed operational data; the mean alone is the tail's accomplice.
